content: Measles outbreaks continue to occur even in countries with high vaccination coverage. Passive immunization is generally used to prevent measles in individuals who are not immune and have been exposed to the virus. However, the effectiveness of this approach has varied, and no minimum effective dose of immunoglobulin has been established. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of immunoglobulins, administered either intramuscularly or intravenously, for preventing measles in susceptible individuals who have been exposed to the virus but have not yet developed symptoms. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, CINAHL, and EMBASE, up to August 2013. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and prospective cohort studies in which participants were susceptible to measles, had been exposed to the virus, and received polyclonal immunoglobulins derived from human serum or plasma as the sole intervention. Studies involving other sources of immunoglobulins were excluded. Two authors independently extracted data and critically appraised the included studies. They also attempted to contact study authors for missing information. The results of studies that could not be included in meta-analyses were described narratively. The review included one RCT, two quasi-RCTs, and 10 cohort studies, involving a total of 3,925 participants. None of the studies were rated as having a low risk of bias across all criteria, and the quality of evidence was considered moderate overall. Seven studies, involving 1,432 participants, assessed the incidence of measles in individuals who received immunoglobulin compared to those who received no treatment. The heterogeneity in results was explained by subgrouping based on the type of blood product used, which served as a proxy for the dose of immunoglobulin. When administered within seven days of exposure, immunoglobulins were effective in preventing measles. Gamma globulin reduced the risk of measles with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.17 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.08 to 0.36). Convalescent serum showed an RR ranging from 0.21 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.29) to 0.49 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.54), and adult serum had an RR of 0.52 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.59). These differences in effectiveness were supported by additional studies not included in the meta-analysis. Two studies, involving 702 participants, found gamma globulin to be more effective than serum, with an RR of 0.56 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.69). Based on three studies involving 893 participants, immunoglobulin was also effective in preventing death due to measles, with an RR of 0.24 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.44) compared to no treatment. Two studies included measles vaccine as an intervention group, but meta-analysis was not possible. Both studies suggested that the vaccine was more effective than gamma globulin. No serious adverse events were reported in any of the included studies, although the reporting of adverse events was generally poor. Non-serious adverse events included transient fever, rash, muscle stiffness, local redness, and induration. The authors concluded that passive immunization within seven days of exposure is effective in preventing measles, reducing the risk for non-immune individuals by up to 83% compared to no treatment. For example, in a population with an attack rate of 45 per 1,000 (as observed in the control group of one study), gamma globulin reduced the absolute risk by 37 per 1,000, with a number needed to treat to benefit (NNTB) of 27. In a population with a higher attack rate of 759 per 1,000 (as observed in another study), the absolute risk reduction was 629 per 1,000, with an NNTB of 2. The dose of immunoglobulin appears to influence its effectiveness, but a minimum effective dose of measles-specific antibodies could not be identified. Passive immunization was also effective in reducing the risk of death from measles by 76% compared to no treatment. However, it remains unclear whether the benefits of passive immunization vary among different subgroups of non-immune individuals exposed to measles. Due to limited evidence comparing the vaccine to passive immunization, no definitive conclusions can be drawn about their relative effectiveness. Additionally, the included studies were not specifically designed to detect adverse events. Future research should focus on evaluating the effectiveness of passive immunization in high-risk populations, such as pregnant women, immunocompromised individuals, and infants. Further efforts are also needed to determine the minimum effective dose of measles-specific antibodies for post-exposure prophylaxis and to compare the relative effectiveness of the vaccine versus immunoglobulin.
